\begin{abstract}
Crowd crushes are driven by local density, yet most camera analytics report only a head count for the whole image. We present CrowdSafe, a pipeline that converts fixed CCTV video into crowd density in \pmsq{} for each floor zone, forecasts it 10--60\,s ahead (120\,s in simulation) and raises tiered alerts with hysteresis, using only pretrained models. A zero-shot CLIP-EBC density map is projected onto the floor through a camera model with lens distortion fitted to furniture of known size; RAFT optical flow supplies motion features; Chronos-2 forecasts each zone zero-shot, and split conformal calibration sets its 90\,\% upper bound. We evaluate on our own classroom CCTV (four cameras, three rooms, 2.6\,h, 6,715 labelled heads), ShanghaiTech, held-out J\"ulich pedestrian experiments and 16 JuPedSim scenarios. CLIP-EBC counts with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 2.0--5.1 people per frame, and zone density is estimated within 0.08--0.10\,\pmsq{} of the labels; a learned detector--density fusion does not transfer to unseen rooms. On held-out test runs the calibrated Chronos-2 bound holds for 89--96\,\% of CCTV and simulation forecasts and 84--93\,\% of J\"ulich forecasts, against 66--85\,\% for persistence on J\"ulich. Because our CCTV never exceeds 3.2\,\pmsq, dangerous densities are evaluated only on J\"ulich and simulation: alerts on current density never warn before a zone reaches 4\,\pmsq, whereas forecast-driven alerts warn in time for 34\,\% of 47 simulated events (median 7.5\,s ahead) and one of nine real events. The live pipeline runs on one A100 GPU with 0.49\,s median latency. The measured warning lead time is seconds, not minutes.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
crowd counting, crowd density estimation, camera calibration, zero-shot learning, time-series forecasting, conformal prediction, optical flow, crowd monitoring, early warning
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Background}
Crowd disasters are caused by local density and the forces it produces, not by the total number of people present. Pedestrian level-of-service analysis and later empirical studies place the onset of dangerous conditions at roughly 4--5\,\pmsq, with stop-and-go waves and turbulent ``crowd quakes'' at higher densities~\cite{fruin1971,helbing2007}. Venues increasingly have fixed CCTV cameras, so the question is whether that existing infrastructure can measure and anticipate dangerous local density.

\subsection{Motivation}
Crowd-counting research and most deployed analytics report people per image~\cite{zhang2016mcnn,li2018csrnet,ma2025clipebc}. A count per image does not tell an operator \emph{where} density is building up, and it cannot be compared with density thresholds without knowing the floor area each part of the image covers. Converting image counts to \pmsq{} requires a camera calibration, which existing installations rarely have. Anticipating, rather than detecting, dangerous density additionally needs a forecaster that works without venue-specific training data, because dangerous events are rare.

\subsection{Problem Statement}
Given an uncalibrated fixed CCTV camera and a few tape-measured dimensions in the scene, estimate the crowd density in \pmsq{} of each floor zone once per second, forecast it over the next minute with a reliable upper bound, and decide when to raise an alert so that staff are warned \emph{before} a zone reaches a dangerous density, with few false alarms. The research questions are how accurately pretrained, zero-shot components can do this, and how much warning time they actually provide. The engineering question of running the pipeline live is treated separately (latency, Section~\ref{sec:runtime}).

\subsection{Objectives}
(i) Measure zone density in physical units from existing CCTV without training a counting model; (ii) forecast zone density with an upper bound whose coverage is verified on held-out data; (iii) evaluate alert lead time and false alarms under a strict protocol on real and simulated dangerous crowds; (iv) measure end-to-end latency on one GPU.

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item A calibration procedure that fits a camera model with radial distortion to desk tops of known length and straight scene edges, validated against tape-measured distances not used in the fit (Section~\ref{sec:res-calib}).
\item A held-out evaluation of zero-shot counting on real classroom CCTV, including a negative result: learned detector--density fusion that is best within one room is worst on unseen rooms (Section~\ref{sec:res-count}).
\item Zero-shot zone-density forecasting with split conformal calibration, evaluated for coverage overall and at high densities (Section~\ref{sec:res-forecast}).
\item An early-warning evaluation with a strict lead-time metric, motion-precursor tests and an ablation of alert timing, reporting that forecast-driven alerts warn only seconds ahead (Section~\ref{sec:res-alerts}).
\item A live implementation with per-stage latency, and a replay dashboard.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}

\subsection{Crowd Counting: Detection versus Density Estimation}
Density-map regression estimates a per-pixel density whose integral is the count. MCNN introduced the ShanghaiTech benchmark with a multi-column network~\cite{zhang2016mcnn}; CSRNet replaced pooling with dilated convolutions on a VGG-16 front end~\cite{li2018csrnet}; CLIP-EBC recasts counting as blockwise classification on a CLIP backbone and reports state-of-the-art accuracy on NWPU-Crowd~\cite{ma2025clipebc,wang2021nwpu}. These methods are trained and evaluated per dataset and report counts per image. Person and head detectors such as YOLO11~\cite{yolo11}, including models trained on CrowdHuman~\cite{shao2018crowdhuman}, count only visible instances; the CrowdHuman authors identify occlusion as the central difficulty of crowded scenes.

\subsection{Crowd Dynamics and Precursors of Crowd Disasters}
Helbing et al.\ analysed video of the 2006 Hajj crowd disaster and described transitions from laminar to stop-and-go to turbulent flow, proposing \emph{crowd pressure}, density times the local velocity variance, as an indicator of danger~\cite{helbing2007}. Controlled experiments by Forschungszentrum J\"ulich provide measured trajectories at high densities~\cite{julich_archive}; open tools exist to analyse such trajectories (PedPy~\cite{pedpy}) and to simulate pedestrian scenarios (JuPedSim~\cite{jupedsim}).

\subsection{Crowd Density and Flow Forecasting}
ST-ResNet forecasts the inflow and outflow of city grid regions from trajectory data~\cite{zhang2017stresnet}. Niu et al.\ forecast the future crowd distribution of a scene from consecutive video frames and their density maps~\cite{niu2020overcrowdedness}. Pretrained time-series foundation models forecast new series without task-specific training: Chronos tokenises values into a language-model vocabulary~\cite{ansari2024chronos}, and Chronos-2 adds group attention so that related series inform each other~\cite{ansari2025chronos2}. Split conformal prediction turns any forecaster's residuals on held-out data into a bound with finite-sample coverage under exchangeability~\cite{angelopoulos2023conformal}.

\subsection{Integrated Crowd Monitoring and Early-Warning Systems}
Cao and Huang describe a video-based system that estimates crowd density over a multi-camera network for wide-area surveillance and predicts it several minutes ahead~\cite{cao2013video}. Niu et al.\ motivate their forecaster with alerts for regions that will become over-crowded~\cite{niu2020overcrowdedness}.

\subsection{Research Gap}
Table~\ref{tab:gap} summarises the reviewed studies. Each addresses part of the problem: image-level counting, empirical crowd dynamics, forecasting on other data types, or system-level prediction. In the sources we reviewed we did not find an evaluation that combines (a)~calibrated density in \pmsq{} per floor zone from an uncalibrated existing camera, (b)~a forecast bound whose coverage is verified on held-out data, and (c)~alert lead time measured with an explicit event protocol on real dangerous crowds. CrowdSafe studies this combination using only pretrained components; we do not claim that the cited systems cannot provide these properties, only that their reported evaluations differ.

\section{Proposed Methodology}
\label{sec:method}

Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline} shows the complete pipeline and the data passed between its blocks. Once per second a frame and a partner frame 0.2\,s later are taken from the video. CLIP-EBC turns the frame into a density map and RAFT turns the pair into an optical-flow field. The offline-fitted camera model provides, for every zone, an image mask and its visible floor area, and maps pixels to the floor. Aggregating the density map and flow inside each zone mask gives one feature row per zone and second. Every 5\,s the last 30\,s of each zone's rows are forecast; the forecast's calibrated upper bound and the current density give a risk level, and an alert manager with hysteresis turns levels into alert events for the dashboard. Rows with the same columns are also built from measured (J\"ulich) and simulated (JuPedSim) trajectories, so forecasting and alerting are evaluated identically on all sources.

\textbf{Notation.} $z$ indexes zones and $t$ seconds. $D_t$ is the density map of frame $t$, $M_z$ the image mask and $A_z$ the visible floor area (m$^2$) of zone $z$, $c_{z,t}$ the zone count and $\rho_{z,t}=c_{z,t}/A_z$ the zone density. A forecast issued at origin $o$ gives quantiles $p^{(10)}_{z,o,h}$, $p^{(50)}_{z,o,h}$, $p^{(90)}_{z,o,h}$ for horizons $h$ in seconds; $q_h$ is the conformal offset and $U_{z,o,h}=p^{(90)}_{z,o,h}+q_h$ the calibrated upper bound.

\subsection{Camera Calibration}
\emph{Input:} still frames of the empty or lightly occupied room and measured dimensions: desk-top length (1.00\,m in the classrooms), table positions and camera height in the computer lab. \emph{Operation:} we fit a pinhole camera with radial distortion coefficients $k_1, k_2$, focal length and pose by robust least squares. In classrooms, desk tops are modelled as parallel rectangles of known length on one plane; each desk has its own unknown floor position, so row and column spacing are \emph{not} assumed and remain independent checks. Straight scene edges (door frames, ceiling duct, stage edge) add plumb-line constraints that fix the distortion. In the lab, long table edges at known lateral positions and vertical edges are used, with a soft prior on the measured camera height. Calibration is checked against measured distances excluded from the fit (Section~\ref{sec:res-calib}) and is treated as approximate. \emph{Output:} a camera model per camera that maps any image point to the floor at a chosen height. \emph{Next consumer:} zone definition (Section~\ref{sec:zones}) and motion conversion (Section~\ref{sec:motion}).

\subsection{Zone Definition and Area Computation}
\label{sec:zones}
\emph{Input:} zone polygons drawn on the floor plan in metres by the administrator, and the camera model. \emph{Operation:} each classroom is divided into 3$\times$3 seating blocks plus the front aisle (4--16\,m$^2$ per zone). Each polygon is projected into the image at seated head height (1.2\,m), because heads, not feet, are what the density map localises; the projected region is the zone mask $M_z$, and $A_z$ is the floor area whose head-height projection is visible in the image. Regions outside the room (a glass partition in the lab) are excluded. \emph{Output:} $M_z$ and $A_z$ for every zone. \emph{Next consumer:} zone density estimation (Section~\ref{sec:density}).

\subsection{People Counting}
\label{sec:counting}
\subsubsection{Density Estimation with CLIP-EBC}
\emph{Input:} the sampled frame $I_t$. \emph{Operation:} CLIP-EBC ViT-B/16 with the authors' NWPU-Crowd weights~\cite{ma2025clipebc,wang2021nwpu}, applied without fine-tuning in 224-pixel sliding windows. \emph{Output:} a density map $D_t$ whose cells hold expected numbers of heads, with the exclusion mask applied. \emph{Next consumer:} zone density estimation.

\subsubsection{Person Detection with YOLO11 (Baseline)}
YOLO11l with COCO weights and a YOLO11 person+head model trained on CrowdHuman~\cite{yolo11,shao2018crowdhuman} are evaluated as counting baselines on the same frames. They return boxes, so their output is a frame count (number of detections) rather than a density map.

\subsubsection{Sparse-Scene Hard Switch}
Detectors can be more accurate than density models in near-empty scenes. The hard switch uses the detector count when the CLIP-EBC frame count is below a threshold $\tau$ and the CLIP-EBC count otherwise; $\tau$ is fitted on the training rooms only. We also tested a constant detector weight, a 50/50 average and a learned per-frame weight from detector-reliability features. These variants operate on frame counts and are evaluated only at frame level (Section~\ref{sec:res-count}). Because zone density requires a spatial map, the zone path uses the CLIP-EBC density map alone.

\subsection{Zone Density Estimation in Persons per \texorpdfstring{m$^2$}{m2}}
\label{sec:density}
\emph{Input:} $D_t$, $M_z$ and $A_z$. \emph{Operation:} $c_{z,t}=\sum D_t\odot M_z$ and $\rho_{z,t}=c_{z,t}/A_z$; zones with less than 2\,m$^2$ visible are skipped. \emph{Output:} the density $\rho_{z,t}$ in \pmsq{} for every zone and second. \emph{Next consumer:} the zone feature table (Section~\ref{sec:table}), where it is the forecasting target.

\subsection{Crowd Motion Feature Extraction}
\label{sec:motion}
\subsubsection{Optical Flow with RAFT}
\emph{Input:} the pair $(I_t, I_{t+0.2\,\mathrm{s}})$. \emph{Operation:} pretrained RAFT-large~\cite{teed2020raft} at 960\,px width. \emph{Output:} a flow field $F_t$ in pixels per frame pair.

\subsubsection{Speed, Speed Variance, and Crowd Pressure}
Flow is averaged per density-map cell; each cell centre and its displaced position are traced through the camera model to the head-height plane, giving a velocity in m/s. Within each zone, cells are weighted by the density map so that empty floor contributes nothing. This yields the mean speed (m/s), the velocity variance (m$^2$/s$^2$, sum of the variances of both components) and crowd pressure $\rho\cdot\mathrm{var}$ (s$^{-2}$)~\cite{helbing2007}.

\subsubsection{Direction Entropy, Counter-Flow, Inflow, and Outflow}
Direction entropy is the normalised entropy of an 8-bin histogram of movement directions, and counter-flow is the share of movement opposite to the zone's mean direction (both in $[0,1]$). Inflow and outflow (persons/s across zone boundaries) require individual trajectories; they are computed for J\"ulich and simulated data from boundary crossings, but not from CCTV, where they are left missing. \emph{Output of this subsection:} the motion columns of the feature row. \emph{Next consumer:} the feature table; the per-zone Chronos-2 variant uses motion columns as covariates, and the precursor tests use them (Section~\ref{sec:precursors}).

\subsection{Zone Feature Table Construction (CCTV, J\"ulich Trajectories, JuPedSim Simulations)}
\label{sec:table}
\emph{Input:} zone density and motion values from CCTV, or trajectories from J\"ulich experiments and JuPedSim runs. \emph{Operation:} every source is converted to one row per (camera or run, zone, second) with the columns timestamp, zone, count, density, mean speed, speed variance, pressure, direction entropy, counter-flow, inflow, outflow and source. For trajectory data, zones are 2\,m$\times$2\,m cells (J\"ulich cells kept when at least 90\,\% walkable; simulated cells use the walkable area excluding furniture); counts are averaged over each second, velocities above 4\,m/s are treated as tracking errors, and our J\"ulich zone densities match PedPy's classic density to 0.0000\,\pmsq{} on six checked runs. \emph{Output:} a time-indexed table at 1\,Hz. \emph{Next consumer:} the forecasters, which read each zone's recent rows as a series.

\subsection{Crowd Density Forecasting}
\label{sec:forecasting}
\subsubsection{Chronos-2 Zero-Shot Forecasting}
\emph{Input:} every 5\,s (forecast origin $o$), the last 30\,s of each zone's rows at 1\,Hz. \emph{Operation:} Chronos-2~\cite{ansari2025chronos2} is applied without training in two variants: \emph{per zone}, one series per zone with density as target and pressure, inflow, outflow and mean speed as past covariates (missing covariates are set to zero, which affects inflow and outflow on CCTV); and \emph{joint}, all zones of a camera as one multivariate series of densities. In the live loop, timestamps are snapped to a 1-s grid and a second skipped by a slow cycle is filled with the previous value, because Chronos-2 requires a regular series. \emph{Output:} quantiles $p^{(10)}, p^{(50)}, p^{(90)}$ per zone and horizon, clipped at zero.

\subsubsection{Baseline Forecasters (Persistence, Physics Fill-Rate)}
\emph{Persistence} predicts the last observed density for all horizons. The \emph{physics fill-rate} model predicts $\rho_{z,t}+(\bar q_{\mathrm{in}}-\bar q_{\mathrm{out}})\,h/A_z$ with inflow and outflow averaged over the last 10\,s; it is evaluated only where inflow and outflow exist (J\"ulich and simulation). Both are point forecasts ($p^{(10)}=p^{(50)}=p^{(90)}$), so their upper bound comes entirely from the conformal offset.

\subsubsection{Prediction Horizon Selection}
Horizons are 10, 30 and 60\,s on CCTV and J\"ulich data, because most J\"ulich runs last only 1--3\,min, and additionally 120\,s on the longer simulations. The 30-s context is the history available shortly after monitoring starts. The forecast horizon bounds the possible warning time but is not the warning time itself; the measured lead time is reported separately (Section~\ref{sec:res-alerts}).

\subsection{Reliable Upper Bound via Conformal Calibration}
\emph{Input:} forecasts and realised densities on the validation split. \emph{Operation:} for each model and horizon, $q_h$ is the finite-sample split-conformal quantile of the residuals (target $-\,p^{(90)}$) at level $\lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil/n$ with $\alpha=0.1$~\cite{angelopoulos2023conformal}; test forecasts receive $U_{z,o,h}=\max(0,\,p^{(90)}_{z,o,h}+q_h)$. Validation and test runs never overlap. \emph{Output:} a calibrated upper bound per zone, origin and horizon. \emph{Next consumer:} risk classification.

\subsection{Risk Classification (Low, Medium, High, Critical)}
\emph{Input:} $U_{z,o,h}$ for all horizons and the current density $\rho_{z,o}$. \emph{Operation:} the worst case $W_{z,o}=\max(\max_h U_{z,o,h},\ \rho_{z,o})$ is mapped to Low ($<2$), Medium (2--4), High (4--5) or Critical ($\geq 5$\,\pmsq). Before the first forecast origin of a run, only the current density is used. The time to critical is the first horizon whose bound reaches 5\,\pmsq. \emph{Output:} a level, time to critical and a short reason (e.g.\ ``forecast upper bound 4.2 \pmsq{} (now 1.8)'') per zone every 5\,s. \emph{Next consumer:} the alert manager.

\subsection{Precursor-Based Risk Escalation}
\label{sec:precursors}
The risk engine can raise a level by one step when a motion precursor fires: pressure, direction entropy or counter-flow above a threshold, mean speed below a threshold, rising density with falling speed (flow collapse), or a fast rate of density rise. A precursor is kept only if, on validation data, its precision for ``the zone reaches 4\,\pmsq{} within 60\,s'' (among zone-seconds at 2--4\,\pmsq) is at least twice the base rate. Pooled over the J\"ulich and simulation validation splits, no precursor passed, so the selected configuration uses none (Section~\ref{sec:res-negative}).

\subsection{Alert Generation}
\emph{Input:} levels per zone every 5\,s. \emph{Operation:} an alert is raised when a zone's level stays at High or above for 10\,s and cleared after 30\,s below High; it carries the zone, the highest level reached, the time to critical and the reasons. \emph{Output:} alert events (raise time, zone, level, reasons). \emph{Next consumer:} the evaluation (Section~\ref{sec:res-alerts}), the live log and the dashboard.

\subsection{Dashboard Visualisation}
A FastAPI/WebSocket server replays stored runs: it loads the feature table and stored forecasts of a run, re-runs the risk engine and alert manager with the same configuration, and streams one message per second to a Next.js dashboard. The dashboard shows the camera video (or a 2-m grid for trajectory runs) with zones coloured by level and labelled with current density, a time bar of peak density, the forecast band of a selected zone and the alert feed (Fig.~\ref{fig:dashboard}). It replays processed recordings; it is not connected to a live camera. The live pipeline (Section~\ref{sec:runtime}) runs the same steps on a stream and logs every stage to SQLite.

\subsection{Own CCTV Recordings and Annotation}
Four fixed cameras in three rooms of our university were recorded with permission: two views of classroom H705, classroom H706 and computer lab H103 (2.6\,h in total), covering lectures, a class leaving, students studying and a lab filling up. Head points were annotated on 160 frames (H705: 100 frames from two views; H706: 30; H103: 30; 6,715 heads) by correcting model pre-labels in CVAT. The highest zone density in the labelled frames is 1.67\,\pmsq, and over the full videos the busiest zone reached 3.2\,\pmsq; the recordings therefore contain no dangerous densities. To our knowledge these recordings have not been used in prior research. No identities, faces or tracks are stored; labels are head points.

\subsection{ShanghaiTech Benchmark}
ShanghaiTech Part A (dense, web images) and Part B (street scenes) were introduced with MCNN~\cite{zhang2016mcnn} and are widely used for counting, e.g.\ by CSRNet~\cite{li2018csrnet}. We use only the test sets, with image-level count ground truth, to check that the zero-shot models behave as expected.

\subsection{J\"ulich Pedestrian Experiments}
The J\"ulich archive~\cite{julich_archive} provides trajectories of controlled experiments. The unidirectional-corridor experiments of 2013~\cite{julich_uni2013} were used by Cao et al.~\cite{cao2017fundamental}, and the entrance experiment with a semicircular crowd~\cite{julich_semicircle} by Sieben et al.~\cite{sieben2017collective}. Splits are by experiment (geometry), never within a run. The test experiments reach 5.3 and 9.0\,\pmsq.

\subsection{JuPedSim Simulated Scenarios}
Sixteen scenarios were simulated with JuPedSim's collision-free speed model~\cite{jupedsim} in four layouts: a classroom modelled on H706, a corridor with a bottleneck, a hall with two exits and a bidirectional corridor, with arrival surges, exit closures and opposing flows. Desired speeds follow a normal distribution with mean 1.34\,m/s and standard deviation 0.26\,m/s (clipped to 0.7--1.9\,m/s)~\cite{weidmann1993}. Ten scenarios exceed 5\,\pmsq{} (maximum 8.0); classroom scenarios stay below 4. Simulations follow model rules, not real behaviour, and are reported separately from real data.

\subsection{Train, Validation, and Test Splits}
Counting uses no training; the fusion parameters ($\tau$ and weights) are fitted leave-one-room-out, on two rooms, and tested on the third. A within-room comparison uses the first half of one H705 view by time for fitting (43 frames) and the rest for testing (57 frames). Conformal offsets are fitted on validation cameras, experiments or scenarios and applied to disjoint test ones. Precursor thresholds are tuned on the pooled J\"ulich and simulation validation splits. Test splits are used for no fitting.

\subsection{Evaluation Metrics}
\emph{Counting:} MAE and RMSE in people per frame. \emph{Zone density:} MAE in \pmsq{} over zone-frames. \emph{Forecasting:} MAE of the median forecast in \pmsq{} per horizon, and \emph{coverage}, the share of test forecasts with realised density $\leq U$ (target 0.90), reported over all test points and over points whose realised density is at least 4 or 5\,\pmsq. \emph{Alerts:} monitoring of a run starts at its first forecast origin. An \emph{event} is the first second at which a zone reaches the event density (4 or 5\,\pmsq) after monitoring starts. An event is \emph{warned in time} if an alert for that zone was raised at most (longest horizon + 10\,s) before it and more than 15\,s after monitoring started (the first forecasts extrapolate the start-up ramp). The \emph{lead time} is the time from that alert to the event. A \emph{false alarm} is an alert with no event-density sample in the zone from 30\,s before to 120\,s after it was raised, reported per zone-hour of monitoring.

\subsection{Hardware and Software}
\label{sec:hw}
Density maps, optical flow, Chronos-2 forecasts and latency were run on one NVIDIA A100 40\,GB shared GPU through Jupyter notebooks, using the authors' PyTorch weights and \texttt{chronos-forecasting}. Counting on the labelled frames used ONNX exports of the models on a laptop CPU. Simulations used JuPedSim 1.4.2 and trajectory analysis PedPy 1.5.1. The global random seed is 42.

\section{Results and Discussion}

\subsection{Counting Accuracy on ShanghaiTech}
Table~\ref{tab:counting} (right column) shows that zero-shot CLIP-EBC reaches an MAE of 66.95 on ShanghaiTech A and 11.66 on B, while the detectors miss most people in these dense images (MAE 374--418 on A). This confirms that the density model works as expected before it is applied to our cameras; it is not a comparison of trained models.

\subsection{Counting Accuracy on CCTV and Fusion Ablation (Leave-One-Room-Out)}
\label{sec:res-count}
On our CCTV (Table~\ref{tab:counting}) CLIP-EBC has the lowest MAE in every room. The detectors undercount (bias $-6$ to $-17$ people per frame in the rooms) because desks, other students and lab monitors hide bodies; in the lab YOLO11l misses about 18 people per frame. Tiling the detector input did not help on ShanghaiTech. Detectors are competitive only in near-empty frames: below 20 people in H705, the head detector's MAE is 0.86 against 1.15 for CLIP-EBC.

Within one room (H705, time split), combining counts looked very effective: a constant detector weight reached an MAE of 1.59 and the learned per-frame weight 2.09, against 5.30 for CLIP-EBC alone, because the two models erred in opposite directions there (+5.1 and $-6.0$ people). Leave-one-room-out reverses this (Table~\ref{tab:fusion}): the learned fusion is the worst combination on unseen rooms (5.22), and only the hard switch improves slightly on CLIP-EBC alone (3.16 vs 3.22, mean over three held-out rooms). We therefore report learned fusion as a negative result and use the CLIP-EBC density map for zone density.

\subsection{Calibration Accuracy}
\label{sec:res-calib}
Reprojection errors are 4.2\,px (H705), 3.6\,px (H706) and 4.0\,px (H103). Checks against measurements excluded from the fit: in H705 the fitted row spacing is 0.99\,m against 0.96\,m measured (+3\,\%) and the mean desk-plus-gap 1.69\,m against 1.77\,m ($-5$\,\%; single gaps $-1$ to $-10$\,\%); in H706 desk-plus-gap is 1.78\,m against 1.77\,m and a door width 1.23\,m against 1.12\,m (+10\,\%); in H103 the edges of the two table columns left out of the fit are found within 0.03--0.18\,m. We therefore treat the calibration as accurate to roughly $\pm 5$\,\%. In H103 the camera height is not an independent check because it enters the fit as a prior.

\subsection{Zone Density Accuracy}
Against the labelled heads placed on the floor through the same camera model, zone-density MAE is 0.101\,\pmsq{} in H705 (1,000 zone-frames; highest true zone density 1.67), 0.081 in H706 (300; 1.40) and 0.078 in H103 (300; 1.29). Of the labelled heads, 94--98\,\% fall inside a zone. Changing the assumed head height from 1.1 to 1.6\,m changes the MAE by at most 0.03\,\pmsq. These errors are small relative to the 2\,\pmsq{} width of the risk bands, but they are measured only up to 1.67\,\pmsq; accuracy at dangerous densities on CCTV remains untested.

\subsection{Forecasting Accuracy and Upper-Bound Reliability}
\label{sec:res-forecast}
Table~\ref{tab:forecast} reports MAE and coverage on the test splits. On average error, Chronos-2 matches persistence and is slightly better on our CCTV (0.064--0.097 vs 0.074--0.105\,\pmsq). The physics fill-rate model has the largest errors and they grow quickly with the horizon. Over all test points, the calibrated Chronos-2 bound is close to the 90\,\% target on all three sources (0.84--0.96), while the persistence bound falls to 0.66--0.68 on J\"ulich at 30--60\,s. The calibration step matters most for point forecasts: persistence's raw bound holds for only 48--50\,\% of CCTV forecasts; the conformal offset raises this to 91--93\,\%.

When only points with a realised density of at least 4\,\pmsq{} are kept (Table~\ref{tab:forecast}, right), coverage falls below the target for every model, because high values are the hardest to anticipate and the calibration is not conditional on density. Chronos-2 still holds 0.76--0.88 on J\"ulich (per zone) and 0.77--0.84 in simulation (joint), against 0.56--0.78 and 0.62--0.71 for persistence. At realised densities of at least 5\,\pmsq{} on J\"ulich, Chronos-2 per zone holds 0.91/0.92/0.97 at 10/30/60\,s (85, 64 and 33 points) against 0.88/0.75/0.88 for persistence. The CCTV test cameras never reach 2\,\pmsq, so high-density coverage cannot be measured on CCTV.

\subsection{Early-Warning Performance (Lead Time and False Alarms)}
\label{sec:res-alerts}
Table~\ref{tab:alerts} reports the strict alert evaluation on the test splits. For the 4\,\pmsq{} event, alerts driven by the current density never warn in time, because they cannot fire before the density itself is high. Forecast-driven alerts warn in time for about one third of the 47 simulated events: Chronos-2 per zone 34.0\,\% with a median lead of 7.5\,s, Chronos-2 joint 29.8\,\% (7.5\,s), and physics 31.9\,\% (25\,s) at more false alarms. The persistence bound does not warn in time for any simulated event. On the nine real J\"ulich events, each forecaster warns in time for one event. Fig.~\ref{fig:timeline} shows the run that contains the Chronos-2 per-zone success: in zone c3\_2 the bound crossed 4\,\pmsq{} and an alert was raised 49\,s before the zone reached 4\,\pmsq, while in zone c2\_3 the alert came 123\,s before the event, outside the 70-s window, and in zone c4\_3 only during the warm-up. Our CCTV test cameras produced no events and no false alarms over 8.6 zone-hours.

For a 5\,\pmsq{} event the picture changes: an alert raised at 4\,\pmsq{} by the current density is itself an early warning for 5\,\pmsq, and current-density alerts warn in time for 38.2\,\% of the 34 simulated events (median lead 5\,s), more often than forecast-driven alerts (23.5--26.5\,\%, median leads 25--47.5\,s). On J\"ulich only two 5\,\pmsq{} events occur, and each method warns for one of them.

The forecast horizon (up to 120\,s) is not the warning time. For the 4-\pmsq{} event, median lead times are 7.5--25\,s in simulation, and each method's single in-time warning on J\"ulich came 4--59\,s ahead. In both sources zones go from safe to 4\,\pmsq{} in roughly 10--20\,s, while the alert design adds a 5-s decision step and a 10-s hold, and the forecaster needs 30\,s of history.

\subsection{Runtime Performance}
\label{sec:runtime}
Table~\ref{tab:latency} reports latency of the live pipeline on the shared A100, with camera cam02 played at real speed. Latency runs from the arrival of the newest frame until zone features, risk levels and alerts are ready, and includes the 0.2-s wait for the second frame of the motion pair. With Chronos-2 the median latency is 0.49\,s and 94\,\% of 1-s cycles finish on time; rare spikes of up to 7\,s came mostly from database writes on the shared server. Processing as fast as possible, 908\,s of video took 196\,s (4.6$\times$ real time). On a laptop CPU the pipeline needs about 19\,s per second of video, so live use requires a GPU.

\subsection{Negative Findings}
\label{sec:res-negative}
\emph{Learned fusion.} The learned per-frame detector weight looked strong within one room because detector and density errors happened to cancel there. On unseen rooms the error balance changes (in the lab the detector misses 18 people per frame), and every fitted weight transfers that room-specific balance; the learned fusion is worst of the combinations (Table~\ref{tab:fusion}). A held-out-room test was necessary to see this.

\emph{Motion precursors.} When tuned on J\"ulich validation runs alone (2,665 zone-seconds, base rate 0.145), slowing below 0.21\,m/s reached a precision of 0.54 (3.8$\times$ the base rate) and direction entropy 0.29 (2.0$\times$), while pressure, counter-flow and flow collapse did not pass. Pooled with the simulation validation runs (base rate 0.205), no precursor passed, which suggests that the simulation model does not reproduce slowing before congestion. The selected configuration therefore uses no precursor. Crowd pressure and turbulence are documented at disaster densities~\cite{helbing2007}; at the densities available here they did not anticipate filling better than chance.

\emph{Alert timing.} An ablation with persistence and physics forecasts (events at least 30\,s into a run, the same events for every variant: 29 simulated, 9 J\"ulich) found no variant that helps every method. A 15-s history improved physics in simulation from 58.6 to 62.1\,\% warned (median lead 25 to 37.5\,s) at more false alarms (1.59 to 2.34 per zone-hour). A 5-s hold with a rate-of-rise precursor and the shorter history raised current-density alerts from 0 to 24.1\,\% and persistence from 0 to 31.0\,\% (0.17 false alarms per zone-hour), but lowered physics to 24.1\,\%. We kept the default (30-s history, 10-s hold). These percentages use a different event set from Table~\ref{tab:alerts} and are not directly comparable with it.

\emph{Scoring.} A first, looser scoring counted alerts raised at the start of monitoring and simply kept on; it reported 56\,\% (J\"ulich) and 86\,\% (simulation) of events warned. The strict protocol reduces these to 11\,\% and about one third; we report only the strict values.

\subsection{Limitations}
Calibration is approximate (about $\pm 5$\,\%) and assumes seated head height. Our CCTV contains no dangerous densities, so danger-level results rely on nine real J\"ulich events and on simulations that follow model rules; the percentages for J\"ulich rest on very few events. CCTV speeds have not been validated against ground-truth trajectories, and inflow and outflow are not measured from CCTV, so the physics forecaster and the inflow/outflow covariates are effective only on trajectory data. Latency was measured with one camera on a shared GPU. A single camera view cannot see the cause of a surge outside the frame.

\section{Conclusion and Future Work}

\subsection{Conclusion}
Pretrained, zero-shot components can turn an existing CCTV camera into zone-level crowd density in \pmsq{} with errors around 0.1\,\pmsq{} in the classroom densities we observed, and the full pipeline runs live on one GPU with sub-second median latency. A conformally calibrated zero-shot forecaster provides an upper bound that holds close to its 90\,\% target overall and degrades less than persistence at high densities. Turning that bound into early warnings works for about a third of simulated dangerous events and for one of nine real events, with warnings seconds rather than minutes ahead.

\subsection{Future Work}
Longer warnings need information from beyond a single view: entrance cameras, gate counters, schedules and neighbouring-zone inflow, which our physics baseline already accepts but CCTV does not yet provide. Further steps are measuring inflow and outflow across zone boundaries from CCTV, validating CCTV speeds against tracked ground truth, recording real or staged crowding at dangerous densities with a calibrated camera, density-conditional calibration of the bound, and a multi-camera latency study.
